catalog_citation: Ford, Kevin. 1993. A preliminary comparison of Kamano-Yagaria. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 24: 191-202.
catalog_locator: p.195 (sec.2, Vowel Deletion), p.197 (sec.3), p.200 (sec.3 item ii), p.201 (sec.6 Conclusion); speaker table p.191 (D2 Sidney Higugipa, village Nupagimi, dialect Yate; 'Yate: 2' idiolects). copy consulted: pp.1, 5, 7, 10, 11 (scan without; pages read as images).
catalog_quote: Vowel Deletion makes crucial reference to the fact that K-Y is a lexical tone language. K-Y is a lexical tone language on the following bases: a. as in every language, each syllable bears a tone (or is spoken at a particular pitch); b. again, as in all languages, there are at least two different tones (some K-Y dialects have two tones, High and Low; others have three, Extra-high, High and Low); c. while some dialects prohibit certain tonal combinations, generally any syllable can bear any tone (which is what makes tone lexically distinctive). [p.195] ... EH tone does not occur in Huva or Yate, and is relatively uncommon in Move and Kami, though it is more common in Kafe. [p.197] ... In Yate approximately 95% of about 500 disyllables collected bear HL tone. Like Huva it lacks the stable/unstable distinction, and *HH combinations are realised consistently as HL. [p.200] ... the operation of tone sandhi across the same boundaries as those exemplified for Move demonstrates that the Yate system of tone is of the same type as that shown for Move even though 95% of the lexicon carries a HL tone pattern. [p.201]
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: The Kamano-Yagaria dialect group (which for Ford includes 'Yate, Ke'yagana, Kanite') is analysed as a lexical tone language; the Yate dialect he recorded has a two-level (H/L) system with no extra-high tone, and about 95% of ~500 disyllables carry a High-Low melody (i.e. overwhelmingly initial-high), with tone sandhi across qualifier+N, NP+NP and N+suffix boundaries. Nothing is said about stress. (For the sister variety Kanite, Young 1962:98-99 and the Kanite OPD 1992 state that the suprasegmental phoneme is lexically placed high tone and that stress always falls on the high-toned syllable.)
new_statements.exceptions: The ~5% of Yate disyllables not bearing HL (LH, LL patterns occur per p.196: 'HL and LH occur in all the dialects, LL occurs in all but Move'); polysyllables show additional tonal variation from compounding (fn.2); functional load of lexical tone is 'relatively low' with inter-speaker variation (fn.5, p.199).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on disyllabic words in citation form (tones verified by whistling); sandhi described at phrase level. Based on two Yate idiolects from one village (Nupagimi).
new_statements.identity_note: No phonological description of Inoke-Yate proper [inok1238] exists in the accessible record. (1) Ford 1993's first-hand 'Yate' data come from two speakers of Nupagimi village (his D2); he uses 'Yate' as the cover term for the 'Yate, Ke'yagana, Kanite' end of the Kamano-Yagaria chain, and his Map 1 places Nupagimi just south-east of the Move (Yagaria) area — by Renck 1975:3 (Keiagana and Kanite lie east of Yagaria, Yate to the north-east) and by Glottolog coordinates that is Keyagana [keya1238] country, so his 'Yate' may be Keyagana rather than Inoke-Yate; unverified either way. (2) The SIL team who actually lived among the Inoke (Gibson & McCarthy, 1981-1993) describe Inoke as a dialect of 'the Kanite language' [kani1286] and published phonology only for Kemeyu Kanite: Young 1962:98-99 ('phoneme of tone.. Minimal word pairs contrast as to the syllables on which the tone is placed.. In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable') and the Kanite OPD 1992 ('Stress occurs on high tone. Kanite has two phonemic tones'), i.e. reading tone language with a stress statement / lexically placed for Kanite. Note the two candidate sources disagree in flavour (Kanite: lexically placed H with minimal pairs; Ford's Yate: ~95% HL on disyllables), so neither can safely be transferred to inok1238 without confirming the variety.

sources.note: First-hand tonal data incl. a 'Yate' dialect (village Nupagimi, 2 idiolects): Kamano-Yagaria 'is a lexical tone language' (p.195); Yate has only High and Low, no extra-high (p.197); 'In Yate approximately 95% of about 500 disyllables collected bear HL tone', no stable/unstable final-tone distinction, *HH > HL (p.200); tone sandhi operates in Yate across the same boundaries as Move (p.201). No statement about stress. Identity of his 'Yate' with Inoke-Yate proper is doubtful (see the note on which variety).

sources.note: KANITE [kmu] (sister variety; Gibson & McCarthy treat Inoke as a dialect of Kanite): sec.3.3 pp.98-99: the one suprasegmental phoneme in Kanite is (high) tone, lexically placed with minimal pairs (ke'na 'skirt' vs 'ke'na 'bamboo'; ta'bene 'tree' vs tabe'ne 'our teeth'); no toneless words; noun tone perturbed by preceding adjective; 'In KANITE also, high tone and stress always occur on the same syllable.' Verified on page scan.
